newsitem.title: USA: Clinton Medicare plan cuts providers too much - Lott.
newsitem.headline: Clinton Medicare plan cuts providers too much - Lott.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, joining growing criticism President Clinton's Medicare plan, complained Monday that it relied too heavily on cuts to health care providers to lower costs.
Clinton last week outlined a plan for $138 million in Medicare cuts over six years, mostly from cuts to hospitals, doctors, managed care plans and other health providers.

The plan would also slightly raise premium payments for recipients and cut Medicare more deeply than the president was willing to advocate last year. It will be sent to Congress next week as part of the White House 1998 budget plan.

While Lott said the plan falls too heavily on providers, he made it clear Republicans would not make the first move to increase premiums for the program's 38 million beneficiaries. Democrats attacked Republicans over Medicare in the November elections, saying their failed 1995 balanced budget plan would have destroyed the federal health programme.
"The final proposal must have some control, some restraint, on both the provider side and the beneficiary side," the Mississippi Republican said after a speech to the American Hospital Association.

He charged that the White House had "ducked" the issue of beneficiary changes. Asked whether Republicans would recommend that wealthy recipients pay more for Medicare or make other such moves, Lott said, "We're not going to do it alone."

Other Republican lawmakers have said in recent days that unless Clinton explicitly calls for changes such as requiring well-off beneficiaries to pay higher premiums for Medicare Part B doctor coverage they will not happen.
Health Secretary Donna Shalala, who also spoke to the AHA, said the White House had decided not to ask Congress to freeze Medicare payments to hospitals next year under its budget.
A federal advisory panel has recommended that hospitals, which have controlled costs, not be given their customary inflationary increase in Medicare payments next year.
"This administration will not propose to freeze your payments," Shalala told the group.

Lott said the White House proposal to cut spending on health maintenance organisations by $46 billion over six years went too far and could make it tough to expand managed care. Asked if Republicans would oppose cuts to managed care plans, he said, "That's very conceivable."

Echoing comments of other lawmakers, Lott said Republicans would try again to pass medical malpractice reform and allow small businesses to pool to buy health insurance. He said Republicans wanted to double federal spending on health research over the next decade.

Shalala released data showing that total U.S. health spending rose 5.5 percent in 1995 to nearly $1 trillion. Medical spending in the public sector grew 8.7 percent while private health spending rose 2.9 percent.
